entries.title: Walk of life: Cubs’ patience at plate paying off as offense heats back up following early-summer slump
entries.summary: <p>Pete Crow-Armstrong is one of baseball’s most exciting players.</p><p>But the thing exciting the Cubs the most about their star center fielder these days?</p><p>It’s not the home runs, the clutch hits, the base-swiping speed or his jaw-dropping defensive ability in the outfield.</p><p>It’s that he’s taking his walks.</p><p>Crow-Armstrong has had an utterly ridiculous month at the plate, carrying an outrageous 1.243 June OPS into Tuesday night’s game against the Padres, a number boosted by his reaching base four times a night earlier <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/06/29/cubs-walk-off-win-padres-seiya-suzuki-mason-miller-pitching-injuries-shota-imanaga-pete-crow-armstrong" >in the Cubs’ walk-off win</a>.</p><p>Crow-Armstrong scored the winning run in the ninth, but the next-day compliments were reserved for what Crow-Armstrong did three innings earlier, drawing a walk against Padres reliever Adrian Morejon, who came in with only seven walks issued in 42 innings this season.</p><p>“We enjoy some of the smaller things,” Cubs skipper Craig Counsell said when asked about Crow-Armstrong’s never-ending exploits, “but that walk [Monday] night against Morejon was a great at-bat where Pete was really in control of the at-bat against one of the best left-handed relievers in the game.”</p><p>His teammates, some pretty top-of-the-line walkers among them, were equally impressed.</p><p>“Those things are just generally a reflection of the confidence he has in his at-bats and the trust to take borderline pitches and really know what he wants to hit,” second baseman Nico Hoerner said. “The walk he had off Morejon last night in a big spot, everyone on their feet, one of the best lefty relievers in the game, just pass it on to the next guy? Impressive.”</p><p>Crow-Armstrong walking isn’t news because it’s new to this team. It’s become a talking point because he’s doing something this group has made a staple of its identity.</p><p>The Cubs, even with their extended period of offensive malaise early in the summer, are baseball’s walk kings, coming into Tuesday with 377 of them, more than 30 more than the next highest team total, owned by the division-leading Brewers.</p><p>The Cubs ranked near the top of the sport in on-base percentage – fifth, with a .336 mark – and led the game with a walk rate of 11.2 percent.</p><p>As the bats have heated up over the last couple weeks, the walks have been part of the recipe. The Cubs walked four times Monday against the Padres after drawing 18 in three games against the Brewers, including a quartet against flamethrower Jacob Misiorowski last Friday.</p><p>During a four-game sweep of the Mets in which they scored 33 runs, the Cubs drew a combined 17 free passes.</p><p>“We have a roster that’s very capable of guys getting on base,” left fielder Ian Happ said Saturday in Milwaukee. “Obviously, we’re up there in the league in on-base percentage, just finding a way to get on base.</p><p>“The [first two games of the Brewers series], though starting pitchers have done a great job against us, the pitch counts have been up there a little bit. We definitely did that in New York, too, and got guys out of the game quick.”</p><p>Crow-Armstrong and first baseman Michael Busch rank in the top 30 in the sport in on-base percentage. Busch and Happ rank in the top 30 in walk rate. Busch, Happ and third baseman Alex Bregman all rank in the top 30 in walks.</p><p>Formerly slumping shortstop Dansby Swanson <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/06/24/cubs-dansby-swanson-grand-slam-two-homers-seven-rbis-pete-crow-armstrong-craig-counsell-offense-mets-doubleheader" >broke out in New York</a>, but even when the numbers were their ugliest, he was proud of a career-best walk rate. Busch, like Crow-Armstrong, has received shoutouts for improving plate discipline – he came into Tuesday with 13 multi-walk games, the second highest total in the National League – even with his power numbers down from a season ago.</p><p>It’s a team-wide thing on the North Side, much like the defense that is the backbone of this squad, and it’s fueled an offensive rebirth in the middle of the season.</p><p>The Cubs came into Tuesday having won 13 of 17 games. In that span, since June 11, they led baseball with 108 runs scored – and 83 walks.</p><p>For all the thrill Crow-Armstrong brings and all the walk-off wins that have sent Wrigley bonkers, it’s the presence of the pedestrian base on balls that figures to be key to the Cubs reaching their championship-level goals.</p>

entries.title: Man charged with hate crime in Lake County for allegedly threatening immigrant and Latino residents
entries.summary: <p>A man is facing hate crime charges for making threats against immigrants and Latino residents of the far north suburbs, according to the Lake County State’s Attorney’s office.</p><p>Derek Webb faces a felony charge for hate crime and a misdemeanor charge of disorderly conduct, according to the office. Webb is accused of making threats against Latino and immigrant community members and posting a bullseye sign with “Good Shot ICE” written over it.</p><p>The Waukegan Police Department, the Lake County Sheriff’s Office, the Gurnee Police Department and the Lindenhurst Police Department were said to have collected evidence across “dozens of scenes,” said Lake County State's Attorney Eric Rinehart. Federal law enforcement was also consulted during the investigation for “threat assessment.”</p><p>"Clear threats of physical violence that are motivated by hatred, bias, or racism must be strongly condemned in the community and responded to by the legal system,” Rinehart said in a statement. “True threats are not protected by free speech, and they are particularly dangerous when they are directed towards groups who are historically and wrongfully attacked.”</p><p>Webb was due in court Wednesday.</p>

entries.title: Bulls crawl into free agency taking care of own and inking Zach Collins
entries.summary: <p>Bryson Graham has spoken with a certain amount of honesty since taking over the vacancy for the executive vice president of basketball operations.</p><p>There’s no fantasy talk of rainbows and unicorns with this current Bulls roster, and there’s no promises of an immediate turnaround in Year 1.</p><p>It’s a roll-up-the-sleeves mentality with a lot of talk about “the foxhole.”</p><p>Heck, that was one of the major reasons Graham went with Tiago Splitter as the coach because he knew he needed a like mind in the process.</p><p>“When you’re going through hard times as a coach, player, front office staff, you’ve got to be in a foxhole with somebody that you trust,” Graham said a few weeks back. “There’s no one more I’d rather be in that foxhole with (than Splitter).</p><p>“Let’s get to work.”</p><p>That work crawled out of the gate on Tuesday evening with NBA free agency tipping off and the Bulls surrounded with smoke but no real fire into the first few hours. After strutting out of the NBA Draft last week with Caleb Wilson (No. 4 overall) and Dailyn Swain (No. 15), it felt like time to spend the $31 million in cap space. That will happen, but the market was slow moving to say the least.</p><p>The Bulls did keep Zach Collins out of free agency by inking him to a two-year, $17 million extension, but the only major churning for the Bulls was the rumor mill, as sources reiterated a report that linked the Bulls to veteran guard Norman Powell, while the Sun-Times learned that the Bulls were in talks with the Cavaliers with speculation of Max Strus returning to his hometown team.</p><p>Both transactions would make sense considering the Bulls aren’t looking for a playoff push with this roster, but because of the new 3-2-1 draft lottery rules, finishing bottom three is less than ideal. The sweet spot for best lottery odds is No. 4 through No. 10.</p><p>Considering the lack of outside shooting the Bulls have, Strus or Powell would not only help in that department but would add spacing to the floor for the young frontcourt to develop. More importantly, both would be solid mentors to a very young roster.</p><p>They each have had doses of “Heat Culture,” and both have shown an ability to guard with physicality. Exactly what Graham and Splitter have talked about when describing the style of play they want from the Bulls.</p><p>So where does that leave the roster on night one of free agency in the wake of a turbulent last week throughout the Association? Like Graham said, the “early stages.”</p><p>Kam Jones, who was acquired in a second-round trade last week, was waived, so that cleared a roster spot.</p><p>Wilson and Swain will get a first glimpse of NBA life – albeit Summer League basketball – and all signs point to forward Noa Essengue joining them after the 2025 first-rounder took a redshirt year to get his ongoing shoulder issue finally addressed.</p><p>And there’s a good chance that Splitter will be coaching the trio – at least for a few games in Vegas.</p><p>August will be huge for the veteran players as they start to gather in Chicago for open runs and scrimmages, but Josh Giddey will be front and center, expected to be cleared for full contact and basketball activity after an offseason ankle surgery.</p><p>First thing first, and that will be navigating a bumpy landscape that saw LeBron James walkaway from the Lakers, while players like Giannis Antetokounmpo, LaMelo Ball, Ja Morant and Kawhi Leonard have been traded.</p><p>Free agency, however, was a slow play compared to past seasons, mostly because there aren’t a lot of teams with money to spend. If anything, Graham was playing Tuesday the right way, letting the market set prices and playing the waiting game.</p><p></p>

entries.title: Colson Montgomery, White Sox pound Orioles to close June with two-game division lead
entries.summary: <p>BALTIMORE — <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" ><u>White Sox</u></a> bats erupted for a seven-run third inning on Tuesday en route to a 9-3 victory, locking up a series win over the Orioles as well as the Sox’ first consecutive winning months since 2021.</p><p>Cleveland’s loss to the Rangers sent the upstart Sox into July with a two-game lead in the American League Central, and a sense that they're just getting started.</p><p>"It's a winning month, but you feel like we weren't really hot this month," manager <b>Will Venable</b> said of a 13-12 June. </p><p>Serving as the leadoff hitter, catcher <b>Kyle Teel</b> drew a walk to open the game and scored on a double by <b>Andrew Benintendi</b> off Baltimore starter <b>Trey Gibson</b>.</p><p><b>Colson Montgomery</b> kickstarted the third frame by walloping his 21st home run of the season 440 feet onto Eutaw Street, a two-run rainbow that made him the first Sox slugger to leave Camden Yards since <b>Adam Dunn’s</b> 2013 moonshot in Baltimore.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">440 feet. 109.1 mph. 🤯 <a href="https://t.co/8SMAg8CIM2">pic.twitter.com/8SMAg8CIM2</a></p>— Chicago White Sox (@whitesox) <a href="https://x.com/whitesox/status/2072098554118549965?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">June 30, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>"I didn’t even think it went over that gate," a modest Montgomery reflected. "I knew I got it pretty good, though."</p><p>The Sox piled on Gibson, who loaded the bases and gave up a two-run single to first baseman <b>Jacob Gonzalez</b> and a three-run bomb to left fielder <b>Junior Perez</b>. Gonzalez later roped a pair of doubles, one for his sixth RBI of the series, and fell a few feet shy of a homer in the ninth.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="es" dir="ltr">Junior Pérez to center! <a href="https://t.co/DQRqyKxBtQ">pic.twitter.com/DQRqyKxBtQ</a></p>— Chicago White Sox (@whitesox) <a href="https://x.com/whitesox/status/2072101271889232127?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">June 30, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p><b>Erick Fedde</b>, making his first start sans opener since June 3, went five innings, giving up three runs on five hits and three walks with three strikeouts. Rookie <b>Tyler Schweitzer</b> pitched four scoreless innings for his first career save and the latest pleasant surprise in a season full of them.</p><p>"It's exactly where we want to be," Fedde said. "Everybody here believes that we can win a division."</p><h3><b>Blazin’ Burke</b></h3><p><b>Sean Burke</b> fanned O’s catcher <b>Adley Rutschman</b> on Monday with a 98.9 mph sinker, the second-fastest pitch Burke has thrown all season.</p><p>It came about two weeks after his fastest, a 99.3 mph four-seamer for a punchout that sealed the Sox’ June 18 win <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/06/18/sean-burke-andrew-benintendi-white-sox-yankees-red-sox-junior-perez-will-venable" >at Yankee Stadium</a>. Burke has hurled his 13 hardest throws of the year over the past month, no small coincidence with one of the righty’s best stretches so far.</p><p>He has racked up 22 strikeouts over his past three outings while lowering his ERA to 3.69 on the season, while his fastball has regularly lit up the radar gun well above his 94.7 mph season average.</p><p>“It just feels a lot easier for me to go out there and just be in the zone,” Burke said of his velocity uptick. “Not only the stuff getting a little bit better, but just the zones I’m throwing it to, the sequencing and all that stuff that goes into it — it's really rewarding to see that that stuff's paying off.”</p><p>Venable called Burke’s fastball “dominant,” but Sox pitching coach <b>Zach Bove</b> said the off-speed command has improved, too.</p><p>“I think the curveball has kind of opened up the avenues,” Bove said. “When guys have to respect that, it opens so many more options to attack guys."</p><h3>Eyes Teeled</h3><p>In his sixth game of the season Monday, Teel showed a keen eye for MLB’s new automated ball/strike system, going 4-for-4 on his challenges of calls by home-plate umpire <b>Bruce Dreckman</b>.</p><p>Teel ascended through the minors using the ABS system, but he’s still getting his feel for it at the big-league level after missing most of the first half with hamstring and knee injuries. The second-year backstop lost his first two challenges after returning.</p><p>“Not playing the game for a while, it’s just like learning that strike zone again, and it’s not easy,” Teel said. “So I feel like it’s just letting it come to me, not forcing anything.”</p><p><b>Illinoisans aplenty</b></p><p>The Sox traded Triple-A reliever <b>Ben Peoples</b> (5-1, 2.39 ERA), a prize in last year’s entries.summary: <p>BALTIMORE — When he arrived on the South Side for the home stretch of the worst season in modern baseball history in 2024, Miguel Vargas was the poster boy for <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" ><u>White Sox</u></a> misery.</p><p>Two years later, the third baseman is drawing MVP chants at the heart of an exciting lineup that’s pushing its contending window wide open well ahead of schedule.</p><p>Vargas' .853 OPS is only part of what has replaced the ‘24 image of a seemingly dejected Vargas, freshly traded from the eventual World Series-winning Dodgers, lost in his thoughts at the end of a lifeless Sox dugout.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">The face of a man who got traded from the Dodgers to the White Sox <a href="https://t.co/0pMAuXPDCx">pic.twitter.com/0pMAuXPDCx</a></p>— Jomboy Media (@JomboyMedia) <a href="https://x.com/JomboyMedia/status/1820818442653450438?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">August 6, 2024</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>By now, more fans are more familiar with the hard-charging 26-year-old whose helmet regularly flies off while sprinting around the bases, not to mention his 19 home runs and 15 doubles, or the .357/.455/.786 tear he’s been on over the past week.</p><p>Vargas’ teammates rave about a player who has emerged as a clubhouse leader. The rest of the league is starting to take notice, too.</p><p>“He’s been insane,” Sox starter Anthony Kay said. “I had never seen him play up until this year and he’s been obviously a huge piece for us.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-470000" name="image-470000"></a> <picture as those shouldered by the likes of Colson Montgomery, Noah Schultz and other foundational, homegrown pieces of rebuild.</p><p>But he’s shattered them through the first half of this season nonetheless, slashing .248/.361/.492 while powering a surprisingly slug-happy squad alongside <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/05/18/munetaka-murakami-colson-montgomery-miguel-vargas-white-sox-home-runs" target="_blank" ><u>Montgomery and the injured Munetaka Murakami</u></a>.</p><p>The Sox were second in MLB with 118 home runs and on pace for 226, which would be their most since 2008 — also the last time a Sox third baseman made the All-Star team (Joe Crede).</p><p>Already surpassing his 16 homers last season when he hit .234/.316/.401, Vargas also leads the Sox’ unofficial <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/06/25/white-sox-coach-jose-leger-baserunning-scoring-chart-miguel-vargas-tristan-peters-will-venable" target="_blank" ><u>in-house scoreboard for hustling on the basepaths</u></a>, all while flashing a reliable if not overwhelming glove and playing in all but two games so far this year.</p><p>“He’s a cornerstone third baseman,” said veteran outfielder Randal Grichuk, who has played with his share of them over the past decade. “He's just a great teammate, great person to be around here pregame with, laughing and telling jokes with. And then obviously he works really hard and it shows out there.</p><p>“But he's as good of a human as he is a baseball player,” Grichuk said.</p><p>Vargas’ blossoming at the plate surely has something to do with an uptick in bat speed to an average of 74.2 mph, a sizable jump from the 70.6 mph he swung last season.</p><p>But it’s also a testament to the adjustments he’s made in his second full season as an everyday player, according to manager Will Venable.</p><p>“He’s been so consistent,” Venable said. “Last year we saw it in flashes, we saw him in some stretches that lasted a little longer, but just wasn’t able to really maintain it… He plays every day and he’s running hard every day, he’s getting on base every day. And he just hasn’t stopped.”</p><p>It’s rubbing off, too. Montgomery credited Vargas’ 11-pitch at-bat ahead of him on Monday for setting up the shortstop’s RBI double.</p><p>“He’s grinding his butt off, making the guy throw his best pitches, and then he leaves something over the plate for me,” Montgomery said. “I just think that’s what everyone does and I think that’s what everyone’s capable of doing.”</p><p>Vargas is focused on that grind, not any All-Star speculation.</p><p>“As a team we've been playing really good and we've got bigger goals than that,” Vargas said. “I'm not a selfish guy, so I want to focus and end this half really strong and entries.title: Red Sox' Willson Contreras, Nats' Cade Cavalli spark benches-clearing brawl
entries.summary: <p>BOSTON — Boston Red Sox first baseman Willson Contreras was tossed for a second straight game on Tuesday after throwing his helmet toward Washington Nationals pitcher Cade Cavalli during a heated exchange that ended with the benches clearing on both sides and multiple ejections.</p><p>Cavalli struck out Contreras looking on a full-count pitch in the top of the fourth. The veteran then yelled, "Sit down boy," at Contreras as Contreras made his way back to the Boston dugout.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Willson Contreras throws his helmet during a benches clearing incident after Nationals pitcher Cade Cavalli told him to “sit down boy” <a href="https://t.co/IBEyYXKReN">pic.twitter.com/IBEyYXKReN</a></p>— Talkin' Baseball (@TalkinBaseball_) <a href="https://x.com/TalkinBaseball_/status/2072115239064089048?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">July 1, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Contreras, who hit a three-run homer off Washington's Miles Mikolas on Monday and celebrated with a massive bat flip that he later apologized for, then approached Cavalli on the mound. The two exchanged words as both dugouts emptied.</p><p>Boston catcher Carlos Narvaez tried to hold Contreras back, but Contreras broke loose long enough to leap and throw his batting helmet in Cavalli's direction.</p><p>Things settled down quickly after that, though the brief dustup ended with Contreras, Boston interim manager Chad Tracy, Boston outfielder Nate Eaton and Mikolas being ejected.</p><p>The early exit was the second in as many nights for Contreras, the first time that's happened to a Red Sox player in the club's 126-year history. The 34-year-old Venezuela native — who acknowledged he is having a difficult time while his native country tries to recover from a pair of devastating earthquakes last week — was ejected in the second inning on Monday for mimicking an appeal call after striking out on a checked swing.<br></p>

entries.summary: <p>The Obama Presidential Center recently opened to great fanfare at a June <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/politics/2026/06/18/obama-presidential-center-opening-jackson-park" target="_blank" ><u>celebration</u></a> that included former presidents, celebrities and hundreds of Chicago residents. While tickets are required to enter the museum, the overall center is open to the public and serves a public purpose, according to the Obama Foundation and other supporters of the space.</p><p>But the debate over whether the former president was entitled to use Jackson Park for his museum was a long and <a class="Link" href="https://news.wttw.com/2020/10/28/south-side-coalition-tells-obama-center-obstructionists-enough-enough" target="_blank" ><u>contentious one</u></a>. Critics opposed the use of space in a historic public park when private alternatives existed.</p><p>These types of legal disputes are far from new. In fact, a prominent Chicagoan from the 1800s likely would have been among the voices of dissent, according to his biographer.</p><p>Aaron Montgomery Ward was responsible for one of the city’s most drawn-out fights over public parkland.</p><p>The name may be familiar from the now-defunct chain of department stores that bore his name after his death, or as the catalog guy who revolutionized mail-order shopping over 150 years ago. His lesser-known legacy, perhaps, is his fight over Grant Park.</p><p>Ward spent 22 years and many thousands of dollars fighting to keep Chicago’s premier downtown park “forever open, clear and free” from buildings. But why did he do it? And why isn’t he celebrated more for his crusade?</p><p>The answer involves Ward’s personal aversion to publicity and his stated desire for accessible greenspace for all residents.</p><div The high court sided with Ward every time, ruling that buildings could only go up in Grant Park with the consent of adjacent property owners, Merrill said.</p><p>Next time you visit Buckingham Fountain, try to imagine the Field Museum there instead, in its intended location. Daniel Burnham and Edward Bennett’s dazzling Plan of Chicago involved an expanded Grant Park, with the Field Museum of Natural History as its centerpiece. At the beginning of two related lawsuits that went to the Illinois Supreme Court, Ward offered the directors of the Field Museum something of a truce: They could build their museum in the middle of Grant Park as long as they stopped there.</p><p>“They wouldn't agree to that,” Merrill said. “They had this vision of Grant Park being filled with lots of neoclassical monumental buildings, and they didn't want Ward messing up their vision.”</p><p>Ward’s decades-long opposition was “far more bitter than I think most people realize,” Allen said.</p><h3><b>Ward’s mysterious motives</b></h3><p>In current value terms, Ward spent over $1 million in legal fees defending Grant Park. But why?</p><p>“For whatever reasons — maybe mixed motives — he was passionate about this,” Merrill said.</p><p>Merrill has considered <a class="Link" href="https://scholarship.law.columbia.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1421&context=faculty_scholarship" target="_blank" ><u>several possible reasons</u></a> for Ward’s litigiousness: that he was an environmentalist ahead of his time; that he was a populist looking out for poor Chicagoans; that he hated noise and disorder; that he was driven by how a particular project would affect real estate value on Michigan Avenue. But Merrill noted that Ward was inconsistent with his interventions. Sometimes he opposed small structures, sometimes large ones, sometimes temporary ones. Perhaps Ward was just competitive.</p><p>“He had achieved great success initially, and he kind of got into it,” Merrill said. “I think he sort of got the taste of blood in his mouth for fighting these cases in court because he was winning so much, and so he just kept doing it.”</p><p>Because of his extreme privacy, both Allen and Merrill note, it’s difficult to pin down Ward’s motives. He wrote no memoirs, he declined write-ups in little books of important Chicagoans and he only gave a single interview to the Chicago Tribune, in 1909 amid his contentious Illinois Supreme Court entries.summary: <p>A man was shot in the head and left in critical condition late Tuesday near 31st Street Beach in the Douglas neighborhood. </p><p>Chicago police said the man was found at about 11:35 p.m. along the 700 block of East 31st Street where police administered aid until Chicago Fire Department personnel arrived and took him to the University of Chicago Medical Center. </p><p>No arrests were made. </p><p>Area 1 detectives are investigating. </p>

entries.title: Man critical following West Ridge stabbing
entries.summary: <p>Police are looking for the attacker who plunged a sharp object into the chest and shoulder of a 26-year-old man, critically injuring him early Wednesday in West Ridge. </p><p>The man was discovered along the 6200 block of North Oakley Avenue at 1:22 a.m., Chicago police said. </p><p>He was taken to Saint Francis Hospital in Evanston, where he was listed in critical conditiion, police said. </p><p>Area 3 detectives are investigating.</p>

entries.summary: <p>A 45-year-old man is accused of fatally shooting a 36-year-old woman in January in Woodlawn. </p><p>Eddie Jenkins is charged with murder in the death of Kiara Jenkins, 36, who was found in an alley in the 6400 block of South Drexel Avenue on Jan. 18., Chicago police said.</p><p>Jenkins, of the 9000 block of South Loomis Street, was also charged with misdemeanor fleeing and eluding police, carrying a concealed firearm in or near a park and a traffic violation, police said.</p><p>Jenkins is due in court for a detention hearing at the Leighton Criminal Court building on the Southwest Side later Wednesday. </p><p>Their relationship was not immediately known.</p><p>Kiara Jenkins, 36,<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/01/20/mom-of-5-shot-killed-in-woodlawn" target="_blank" > was found in an alley</a> in the 6400 block of South Drexel Avenue about 4:30 a.m. on Jan 18, officials said. Jenkins, who lived in the Washington Heights neighborhood, suffered multiple gunshot wounds to the body and was pronounced dead at the scene.</p><p>Jenkins has five children, said Ald. Jeanette Taylor (20th) at the time. Jenkins’ home and the alley where she was shot are in Taylor’s district.</p><p>“Her children are now left without their mother,” Taylor said in a statement at the time. “No words can lessen that pain, but it is important to say clearly that her life had value and her family deserves support, compassion and justice. Our children and families deserve protection, stability and the chance to live without fear.”<br></p>

entries.title: Two shot, one fatally in predawn attack outside River North hotel
entries.summary: <p>A shooting early Tuesday outside a River North hotel has left a 30-year-old man dead and a 65-year-old wounded.</p><p>Chicago police said the two men were outside along the busy intersection of Grand Avenue and State Streets about 3:20 a.m. when they someone opened fire and they were shot.</p><p>The 30-year-old man suffered multiple gunshot wounds to his body and was taken to Northwestern Memorial Hospital in critical condition, where police said he was later pronounced.</p><p>The 65-year-old man suffered two gunshot wounds to the foot and was taken to Northwestern Memorial Hospital.</p><p>Dozens of shots were fired and yellow evidence markers could been seen outside the Royal Sonesta River North hotel, 505 N. State St.</p><p>No further information was available, according to police. </p><p>Area 3 detectives are investigating.</p>

entries.title: Celebrating the nation's strengths, beauty for the big 2-5-0
entries.summary: <p>You want to spend your holiday grumbling about America's shortcomings? Well, it’s a free country. Me, to start, I'm toasting our four freedoms — free speech, freedom of worship and freedom from want and fear. And the country's huge land mass and natural resources, from which much additional good derives. And diversity wrought from heavy immigrant traffic. And equality, opportunity and tolerance. What nation over the last quarter-millennium has offered more?</p><p>I also am pondering significant sites like the Valley Forge, where our frostbitten forebears summoned the resolve to see the revolution through. Ditto the Alamo, where Americans faced hopeless odds against Mexican forces, Gettysburg, the Civil War’s climax, and New York City, where the horrific 9/11 attacks unfolded. I also am thinking about contrasting, peaceable marvels like DuSable Lake Shore Drive, Niagara Falls, Yellowstone National Park and Disneyland.</p><p>I'm recalling the Founding Fathers, like Illinois' native son Abe Lincoln, the Roosevelts, Henry Ford, Thomas Edison, Mother Frances Xavier Cabrini, Charles Lindbergh, Audie Murphy, Jonas Salk, John Glenn, John F. Kennedy, Martin Luther King Jr. and many more role models.</p><p>Lincoln's <a class="Link" href="https://www.loc.gov/resource/rbpe.24404500/?st=text" target="_blank" >Gettysburg Address</a> cited the difficulty of honoring such luminaries who've surpassed us. Employing only 272 words, the beleaguered president conceded that the valorous actions at this Pennsylvania crossroads spoke louder than anything we could ever say of them. And likewise with 250th semiquincentennial anniversary, our ineffectual tributes will be quickly forgotten. But we deliver them anyway. It's a necessary part of immortalizing our heritage.</p><p><i>Tom Gregg, Niles</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-670000" name="module-670000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Not feeling this year’s milestone July Fourth </h3><p>Those of us who were around, remember being so excited for the nation’s 200th anniversary in 1976? I was turning 16 that June, and I couldn’t wait for the parades, celebrations and fireworks. What a day to look forward to! Donald Trump has put a damper on this year's milestone with his “Freedom 250” events that are all about him. I don’t want to buy anything that says “250th anniversary” because it reminds me of Trump. I can only look forward to the 275th anniversary of this great nation (God willing) and hope Trump’s grandson or granddaughter is not the president.</p><p><i>Linda Padgurskis, Clearing</i></p><h3>Treaty of Paris marks America’s true birthday</h3><p>The United States, with its post-Revolutionary War independence and nationhood recognized by England, was <a class="Link" href="https://www.bostonteapartyship.com/american-revolution" target="_blank" >“born” in 1783</a>.</p><p>July 4, will not be the U.S.’ 250th birthday. That marks the semiquincentennial of the signing and issuing a Declaration of Independence from the British Crown and Empire by delegates from the 13 colonies. That document began the yearslong trans-Atlantic war between the colonies and the "mother" country. Independence and nationhood lay seven years in the future.</p><p>The battle for separation, recognition and national independence had a long gestation period and a difficult pregnancy. It was difficult; success was not likely until after the colonies’ rebellion began in 1776. We forget the struggles, losses and gains in our rush and misrepresentation under the current national administration.</p><p>British Gen. Charles Cornwallis surrendered to the rebels after the <a class="Link" href="https://www.americanhistorycentral.com/entries/battle-of-yorktown/" target="_blank" >Battle of Yorktown</a> on Oct. 19, 1781. But, critically, the <a class="Link" href="https://www.archives.gov/milestone-documents/treaty-of-paris" target="_blank" >Treaty of Paris</a> — granting independence to the new nation of former colonies — was not signed until Sept. 3, 1783. Almost three more months passed before the last British troops <a class="Link" href="https://thenewleafjournal.com/history-of-new-yorks-evacuation-day/" target="_blank" >left from the port of New York City</a> on Nov 25, 1783.</p><p>The Treaty of Paris, whose 250th anniversary our country should be celebrating, granted full independence and recognized its geographic borders.</p><p>Worthy of note, the U.S. Continental Congress did not officially ratify the <a class="Link" href="https://constitutioncenter.org/blog/on-this-day-congress-beats-deadline-to-end-revolutionary-war" target="_blank" >Treaty of Paris </a>until Jan. 14, 1784. Five more years passed before the U.S. Constitution replaced the Articles of Confederation on March 4, 1789. A month before, the male electorate chose George Washington as the first U.S. president </p><p>In the historical path to independent nationhood, 1783 demands greater commemoration than 1776. I will celebrate the U.S.’ 250th in 2033, when Donald Trump will not be rewriting history.</p><p>The violent theft of the lands and rights of previous sovereign Indigenous nations deserves its own attention in both 2026 and 2033. Both the Declaration of Independence and the Treaty of Paris, which greatly expanded the new nation, ignored Native American rights.</p><p>I urge others to join me in recognizing American independence with respectful historical accuracy. Is patience an American virtue in 2026 like it was in 1776?</p><p><i>Harvey J. Graff, Lincoln Park</i></p><h3></h3><h3>Founding Fathers were ‘No Kings’ guys </h3><p>As we celebrate the 250th anniversary of the <a class="Link" href="https://www.archives.gov/founding-docs/declaration-transcript" target="_blank" >Declaration of Independence</a>, we should not just look at the most quoted excerpts but look at it as a whole, especially those portions that touch on the tyranny of King George III.</p><p>"He has forbidden his Governors to pass Laws of immediate and pressing importance, unless suspended in their operation till his Assent should be obtained; and when so suspended, he has utterly neglected to attend to them," one part reads.</p><p>A few paragraphs later, it says of George III, "He has endeavoured to prevent the population of these States; for that purpose obstructing the Laws for Naturalization of Foreigners; refusing to pass others to encourage their migrations hither, and raising the conditions of new Appropriations of Lands."</p><p>Those who signed the Declaration of Independence wanted leaders of the colonies to have the authority to enact laws. As the <a class="Link" href="https://constitution.congress.gov/constitution/amendment-10/" target="_blank" >10th Amendment</a> of the Constitution, says “The powers not delegated to the United States by the Constitution, nor prohibited by it to the States, are reserved to the States respectively, or to the people.” The Constitution also gives the states the primary responsibility to set the methods for holding congressional elections.</p><p>The Founding Fathers, who clearly didn't want egomaniac kings, also wanted to encourage migration and the naturalization of foreigners.</p><p>To celebrate and honor the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence, Americans should rededicate themselves to the goals set by the founders that were viewed as guarding against tyranny.</p><p><i>Alan Rhine, Glenview</i><br></p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Sister has revealed her true colors time and again
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> When I was 16 and my sister "Daisy" was 18, I found out she was in a sexual relationship with my boyfriend, "Tyler" (also 18). I broke it off. She then asked if I minded her dating him. I'm sure I said I didn't, but I thought, "Why ask? You were already having sex with him." (He and I hadn't.) Tyler and I remained friends through the years. He was my first love.</p><p>That episode shaped my dating relationships going forward. It took years for me to learn to trust again. Years later, I asked Daisy why she'd done that, and her response was because she could. We enjoy each other's company as long as I don't let the past into my consciousness.</p><p>How do I let this go? Saying anything may make things worse — but it really hurts that she betrayed me and never once offered an indication of an apology. — <i>STILL MATTERS IN NORTH CAROLINA</i></p><p><b>DEAR STILL MATTERS:</b> Daisy and Tyler both betrayed you. What they did showed a distinct lack of character on both their parts. But this is who they are. You and your sister may enjoy each other's company, but do not think that the core of her — her character — has changed. That she hasn't apologized for hurting you, and her answering you in such a flip manner, should serve as a warning about how selfish and insensitive she is to this day.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I don't live in the same state as my sister, so I used to call her at the same time each week so we could catch up. Her husband, "Dale," was usually at work on the day I called. Then, Dale got a new job, so he is now home whenever I call.</p><p>My problem is that Dale enters the room and talks to her while she is on the phone. She answers him immediately, even if I am in the middle of a sentence. Because this is confusing and annoying, I told her it would probably be better if she called me when she was free to talk. (At no time did I specifically say anything about Dale's interruptions.) She said, "Fine!" — and that was the last time I heard from her, and it's been more than five months.</p><p>If I reach out to her, I'm sure nothing will change. If I say it's annoying to allow Dale to interrupt phone calls, she'll probably get angrier and defend him. I love my sister and miss talking to her. Must I resign myself to never hearing from her again? — <i>SIS INTERRUPTED</i></p><p><b>DEAR SIS:</b> Call your sister and apologize for letting the silence go on so long. It doesn't matter how rude she and Dale have been; you need to start communicating again if you want to fix this.</p><p>Then, instead of placing all of the responsibility on your sister, why not show her you're willing to compromise? Now that Dale's work schedule is predictable, ask your sister to suggest a time for the weekly call when she knows he won't be around. If that's not possible, you'll have to decide whether Dale's interruptions are annoying enough to lose a sister over.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren, also known as Jeanne Phillips, and was founded by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 69440, Los Angeles, CA 90069.</i></p><p>What teens need to know about sex, drugs, AIDS and getting along with peers and parents is in "What Every Teen Should Know." Send your name and mailing address, plus check or money order for $8 (U.S. funds) to: Dear Abby, Teen Booklet, P.O. Box 446, Kings Mills, OH 45034-0446. (Shipping and handling are included in the price.)</p>

entries.title: America's 250th birthday has arrived. Here's how to celebrate in the Chicago area
entries.summary: <p>After months of planning, the Prairie State is ready to usher in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/arts-and-culture/2026/04/02/america-250-illinois-chicago-federal-national-endowment-arts-trump" >the nation’s semiquincentennial</a> with celebratory events and thought-provoking programs. Those who live in the Chicago area can choose from a number of exhibits, concerts, panels and parties; here are 15 events to consider, with many happening this weekend and throughout July.</p><p>With its debut coinciding with America’s 250th birthday, the <a class="Link" href="https://tinleyparkcountryfest.com/" target="_blank" ><b><u>Tinley Park Country Fest</u></b></a> will offer three days of country music, food, rides and fireworks. Entertainers include Ashley Walls, Eric Chesser, The Morgan Wallen Experience and the Knievel Daredevil Band, with Evel Knievel’s granddaughter, Kelly Knievel. July 3-5. <i>18001 S. 80th Ave. Admission: $18.39 each day for non-residents; Tinley Park residents get in free on Saturday and for half off on Friday and Sunday.</i></p><p>For its “Independence Day Salute,” the <a class="Link" href="https://www.grantparkmusicfestival.com/events/independence-day-salute/" target="_blank" ><b><u>Grant Park Music Festival</u></b></a> will present favorites from Copland and Sousa. The program also includes Gershwin’s “Three Preludes” with principal clarinetist Dario Brignoli and Carlos Gardel’s “Tango (Por Una Cabeza)” with concertmaster Jeremy Black. <i>July 4. Jay Pritzker Pavilion in Millennium Park, 201 E. Randolph St. Admission: free lawn seating, reserved seating varies.</i></p><p>The newly opened <a class="Link" href="https://www.obama.org/" target="_blank" ><b><u>Obama Presidential Center</u></b></a> will kick off its “You Are America” series with “The People’s Fourth,” a free July 4 party featuring live music and activities. Admission: $14 online, $16 at the door.</i></p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://www.newberry.org/" target="_blank" ><b><u>Newberry Library’s</u></b></a><b> </b>commemorative programming runs throughout summer, with an exhibit on the Declaration of Independence and a live reading of the historic document on July 8. Other highlights include an exhibit on wartime political illustrations and a Newberry Fest event featuring Revolution-era items. <i>Through Sept. 19. 60 W. Walton St. Admission: free.</i></p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagobotanic.org/" target="_blank" ><b><u>Chicago Botanic Garden</u></b></a> will explore the history of gardening in the U.S. with its series, “America Grows: 250 Years of Garden Stories.” The organization will offer themed panels, exhibitions and walking tours. Visitors can view the first-known American cookbook and see crops grown in victory and post-emancipation gardens. <i>Through Sept. 30. 1000 Lake Cook Road. Free with admission.</i></p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagoparkdistrict.com/america-250" target="_blank" ><b><u>Chicago Parks District</u></b></a> is using its Night Out in the Park programming to commemorate the nation’s semiquincentennial. Branded as “America 250: Chicago’s Parks, America’s Stage,” the events will include live music, spoken word, theater, dance and more. <i>Through Oct. 10. Various locations. Admission: free. </i></p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://www.architecture.org/" target="_blank" ><b><u>Chicago Architecture Cente</u></b><u>r</u></a> will highlight the city’s role as a “manufacturing and railroad hub” during Open House Chicago, which showcases notable architectural sites through public tours. <i>Oct. 17-18. Various locations. Admission: free.</i></p><p>Influential American artists will be honored with 10-foot sculptures as part of “<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/art/2026/06/05/walking-with-giants-mac-art-center-sculptures-college-dupage" target="_blank" ><u>Walking with Giants</u></a>,” an outdoor exhibition presented by the <a class="Link" href="https://www.theccma.org/" target="_blank" ><b><u>Cleve Carney Museum of Art</u></b></a>, McAninch Art Center and College of DuPage Foundation. Chicago’s Judith Mayer and Naperville’s Rich Lo designed the works, which depict Dolly Parton, Lin-Manuel Miranda, Jean-Michel Basquiat and more. <i>Through Oct. 18. McAninch Art Center, 425 Fawell Blvd., Glen Ellyn. Admission: free.</i></p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://www.chipublib.org/chicago250/" target="_blank" ><b><u>Chicago Public Library</u></b></a> is honoring America’s 250th birthday with exhibitions, book clubs, films, craft workshops and more. The organization is also spearheading “<a class="Link" href="https://www.chipublib.org/news/write-a-letter-to-america/?_gl=1*1qcuvxx*_ga*MTMxNjAyNjM4NS4xNzgyODQzMTc5*_ga_G99DMMNG39*czE3ODI4NDMxNzgkbzEkZzEkdDE3ODI4NDQzOTgkajIxJGwwJGgw*_ga_92RPWHE421*czE3ODI4NDMxNzgkbzEkZzEkdDE3ODI4NDQzOTgkajIxJGwwJGgw" target="_blank" ><u>Letters to America</u></a>,” a citywide initiative that encourages residents 18 and older to write about their experiences, criticism and hopes. After the Aug. 31 deadline, the letters will be archived at the Northside Neighborhood History Collection at Sulzer Regional Library. <i>Programming runs throughout the year. Various locations. Admission: free.</i><br></p>

entries.title: Laws on cocktails-to-go, cyberbullying and new rules for older motorists take effect
entries.summary: <p>A pandemic-era law that made mixed drinks and single servings of wine available for pickup and delivery is one of many laws set to take effect Wednesday.</p><p>In addition to cocktails to-go, Illinois residents will see laws affecting drivers, schools, and the creation of new state agencies.</p><p>Here’s what you should know about some of the new laws taking effect: </p><h3>Cocktails-to-go</h3><p>In June of 2020, Gov. JB Pritzker signed a law that allowed the sale of cocktails by bars and restaurants with liquor licenses for pickup and delivery. It was aimed at keeping businesses afloat during the pandemic while lockdowns kept people from going out to eat or drink.</p><p>Last December, Pritzker made the practice a permanent fixture in Illinois law. And starting July 1, <a class="Link" href="https://my.ilga.gov/Legislation/BillStatus?DocNum=618&GAID=18&DocTypeID=SB&LegId=158316&SessionID=114" target="_blank" ><u>Senate Bill 618</u></a> allows restaurants and bars to offer cocktails and single servings of wine to-go.</p><p>One of the bill’s sponsors, state Sen. Sara Feigenholtz, D-Chicago, said the law presents an opportunity for businesses to continue improving after the pandemic.</p><p>“It is quite an investment for our retail establishments and restaurants to follow,” Feigenholtz said. “I think it allows them to reinvent how they market this.”</p><p>The law also outlines requirements for how the drinks can be distributed. Only a trained employee of the business can deliver the drinks, and it must be transported somewhere in the delivery driver’s car where anyone else in the vehicle can’t access it. Drinks must also be packaged in a sturdy, sealed container with no openings.</p><h3>Safeguarding students </h3><p>Lawmakers also passed several bills in the spring aimed at protecting students. One bill expands the definition of cyberbullying to include artificially generated images.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://my.ilga.gov/Legislation/BillStatus?DocNum=3851&GAID=18&DocTypeID=HB&LegId=162743&SessionID=114" target="_blank" ><u>House Bill 3851 </u></a>adds posting unauthorized AI-generated images to the list of tools that are used for cyberbullying.</p><p>State Rep. Janet Yang Rohr, D-Naperville, one of the sponsors of the bill, said it stems from male students making deepfake images of their female classmates.</p><p>“The use of these exploitative AI apps is so new that what we were finding are schools that were unprepared to address the issue,” Yang Rohr said.</p><p>She said the bill allows for schools to make rules governing the use of these new AI apps.</p><p>“It gives a framework for investigating and addressing the issues, and what kind of policies can schools put in place to prevent this sort of thing,” she said.</p><p>Another bill would keep a student’s record of receiving special education services confidential. Previously, a student’s private “permanent record” only included personal information like their name, age and birth date, guardian’s names and addresses, and attendance.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://my.ilga.gov/Legislation/BillStatus?DocNum=408&GAID=18&DocTypeID=SB&LegId=158032&SessionID=114" target="_blank" ><u>Senate Bill 408 </u></a>adds a summary of a student’s performance that benefited from special education services to the list of private information kept on a student’s “permanent record.”</p><h3>New rules for older motorists</h3><p>Under <a class="Link" href="https://my.ilga.gov/Legislation/BillStatus?DocNum=1226&GAID=18&DocTypeID=HB&LegId=157017&SessionID=114" target="_blank" ><u>House Bill 1226</u></a>, older drivers will also be able to wait a few more years before having to retake their driver’s test or renew their license in person.</p><p>Motorists between the ages of 79 and 86 must renew in person and complete a vision test, but they are no longer required to take a driving test. Previously, that requirement kicked in at age 75.</p><p>Drivers age 87 and older will continue to still have to renew annually and complete both a vision test and a driving test.</p><h3>New state agencies</h3><h3></h3><p><a class="Link" href="https://ilga.gov/Legislation/BillStatus?DocNum=1&GAID=17&GA=103&DocTypeID=SB&LegID=142592&SessionID=112" target="_blank" ><u>Senate Bill 1 </u></a>creates the Illinois Department of Early Childhood to consolidate services that were previously spread among several agencies. The new department will be responsible for oversight and licensing of early childhood education services like preschool and daycare centers.</p><p>The department will receive over $2 million from the state budget.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://my.ilga.gov/Legislation/BillStatus?DocNum=3363&GAID=18&DocTypeID=HB&LegId=161896&SessionID=114" target="_blank" ><u>House Bill 3363</u></a> creates the Office of State Public Defender. The bill requires an 11-member commission to be appointed by Oct. 1, which will be responsible for determining the funding and costs associated with operating the new office.</p>
